items.title: Hypercomplex Method for Solving Nonlinear PDEs
items.summary:
A hypercomplex method for constructing solutions of a class of nonlinear partial differential equations is developed. A family of two-dimensional commutative associative algebras is introduced in which the structural coefficients depend on a component of the monogenic function itself.

A corresponding theory of monogenic functions is developed, and nonlinear analogues of the Cauchy-Riemann conditions are obtained. It is shown that the first component of a monogenic function satisfies a broad class of second-order nonlinear partial differential equations whose coefficients depend on the unknown function.

A hodograph transformation is used to linearize the nonlinear Cauchy-Riemann system. As a result, the problem of constructing solutions of the nonlinear equations is reduced to solving a second-order linear partial differential equation with variable coefficients, followed by the inverse hodograph transformation.

A local correspondence between solutions of the nonlinear Cauchy-Riemann system and solutions of the associated linear equation is established, yielding a constructive algorithm for generating solutions of the original nonlinear PDEs. Several examples are presented in which explicit and implicit solutions of nonlinear second-order PDEs are obtained by this method.

items.title: The Bourgain Project
items.summary:
[This is a guest post by Lukas Liehr , João Pedro Ramos and Mitchell Taylor – T.]

We are launching the Bourgain Project, a community-driven initiative to revisit, expand upon, and explore the body of work of Jean Bourgain, one of the most prolific mathematicians of his time. The goal of this initiative is to develop a deep, comprehensive understanding of each one of Bourgain’s over 500 individual papers, while discussing and connecting the common threads and unifying ideas that run throughout his research.

Bourgain made numerous contributions across many fields, such as harmonic analysis, number theory, partial differential equations, and functional analysis. However, many of his papers are notoriously difficult to grasp. Our initiative aims to make his ideas more accessible to the broader mathematical community.

In addition to digesting Bourgain’s contributions, another main goal of the project is to explore new formats for presenting mathematics beyond the traditional journal article. We encourage contributors to share digestions and expositions of his papers in whatever form, to collaborate in groups, and to engage in discussions on our community Zulip channel.

For more information, we invite anyone interested to visit our website at https://bourgain-pedia.com/ , and check out our latest article digestions.

items.title: The two-step spectral locus of the octonionic structure operator
items.summary:
We continue the study of the octonionic spectrum of the octonionic structure operator $h$ on $W=\mathbb O\otimes_{\mathbb R}V$, where $V$ is the seven-dimensional representation of $G_2$. The real spectrum and the octonionic one-step spectrum, given by the equation $h(w)=wλ$ for real or octonion $λ$, have been determined in earlier work.

In this paper, we study the two-step equation $h(w)=(wλ_1)λ_2$. Due to non-associativity, this does not in general reduce to the one-step problem.

An adapted quaternionic frame represents successive right multiplication by an operator with four real coefficients. The $SU(2)$ subgroup fixing the frame splits $W$ into invariant sectors of dimensions $16$, $12$ and $28$.

We factor the determinant of the resulting 4-parameter operator pencil and characterize the pairs for which a nonzero solution exists. The singular locus of this pencil in $\mathbb R^4$ is the union of an explicit algebraic set and a round $3$-sphere.

The $12$-dimensional sector carries the one-step problem at the reversed product $λ_2λ_1$. The $28$-dimensional sector contributes no additional real singular points; the fixed sector produces solutions even when neither product lies in the one-step right spectrum.

items.title: Degree Bounds for Separating Polynomial and Neural Invariants for Point Clouds
items.summary:
Neural networks that respect the symmetries of point clouds commonly compute high-order representations of the rotation group to improve their expressivity. Such models are known to be universal, and thus able to separate any pair of point clouds, when using representations of sufficiently high order, yet no precise bound on this order, as a function of the number of points, was previously known.

We establish the first quadratic lower and upper degree bounds for polynomials that separate point clouds of n points up to rotations and permutations. By showing Tensor Field Networks and MACE can express all invariant polynomials of a given degree with sufficient representation order, we additionally derive the first explicit, quadratic bound on the representation order sufficient for these architectures to be complete, replacing previous existence results with concrete guarantees.

We further show that, under local regularity assumptions, point cloud separation can be achieved with a message-passing-based model using invariants whose degree depends only on the size of a local neighborhood, rather than on the size of the full point cloud. Finally, we provide counterexamples showing MACE must compute high order irreducible representations to separate locally regular point clouds.

items.title: Saturation degree of powers of graded ideals
items.summary:
Let $I$ be a non-nilpotent graded ideal of a standard graded algebra over a Noetherian commutative ring.

We show that the saturation degree sdeg $I^n$ is asymptotically a constant function or a linear function whose slope is one of the generating degrees of $I$.

Furthermore, we give sufficient (and necessary) conditions for a numerical functions to be the function sdeg $I^n$ of an ideal $I$ generated by forms of the same degree.

Our results may provide a better understanding of the initial behavior of the regularity function reg $I^n$.

items.title: A Non-linearizable Action of $S_3$ on Free Metabelian Lie and Associative Algebras
items.summary:
Let $M$ be the free metabelian Lie algebra of rank $4$ over the field of complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$.

We construct a non-linearizable action of the symmetric group $S_3$, the smallest nonabelian group, on $M$ by automorphisms.

We also construct a non-linearizable action of $S_3$ on free metabelian associative algebras of rank $4$.

items.title: New Maximum Hermitian $d$-Codes and New Invariants from Skew Polynomial Rings
items.summary:
Maximum rank-distance codes were introduced independently by Delsarte (1978) and Gabidulin (1985) for unrestricted matrix spaces, and their study was subsequently extended to the classical form spaces of alternating, symmetric, and Hermitian matrices. For Hermitian $d$-codes, Schmidt (2018) established the upper bound and constructed optimal additive codes for all admissible parameters except when $n$ and $d$ are both even and $4\le d\le n-2$.

We settle this final open existence case, more generally, construct additive maximum Hermitian rank-metric codes for every admissible length and minimum distance. Rather than working directly in the space of Hermitian matrices, we construct our objects within central simple algebras with unitary involution arising from quotients of skew polynomial rings.

We also introduce scalar-field and Lyapunov operators in these algebras, leading to new invariants for the equivalence of additive Hermitian codes. Explicitly determining these invariants yields strong necessary conditions for Hermitian equivalence and demonstrates that our construction contains a large number of pairwise inequivalent codes.

items.title: Dual Reflection Groups from Solutions to the Yang--Baxter Equation
items.summary:
Suppose that $r: X^2 \to X^2$ is a nondegenerate, involutive solution to the set-theoretic Yang--Baxter equation.

To this data, we can associate an Artin--Schelter regular algebra $A$ and an infinite family of groups $G_k$, where $k \geqslant 1$.

For each $k$, we show that $G_k$ is a dual reflection group for $A$, in the sense the component of $A$ graded by $1_{G_k}$ is again Artin--Schelter regular.

We also show that, using the additional structure afforded by the underlying solution to the Yang--Baxter equation, one can determine the centre, Koszul complex, and associated twisted superpotential for $A$.

items.title: Twisted logarithmic de Rham complexes and the rational hit conjecture
items.summary:
We study the top degree concentration property for the cohomology of twisted logarithmic de Rham complexes of multiarrangements of hyperplanes.

Our main tool is a short exact sequence of twisted logarithmic de Rham complexes based on the deletion-restriction exact sequences for logarithmic differential forms found recently by Abe and Denham.

We prove a number of general results that can be used to establish the top degree cohomology concentration property, and also establish that property for some families of multiarrangements.

As a consequence of our results, we prove the rational hit conjecture of R.~M.~W.~Wood about the coinvariants of the rational Steenrod algebra acting on the polynomial ring.

We also make progress on the deformed version of that conjecture proposed by Hivert and Thiéry, prove generalizations of the rational hit conjecture for all complex reflection groups $G(m,p,n)$, thus answering questions of Bergeron, Borie and Thiéry, and generalize the rational hit conjecture to all standard subalgebras of the rational Steenrod algebra.

items.title: Herzog Class of Codimension $3$ Licci Monomial Ideals
items.summary:
Let $S$ be the polynomial ring in three variables with homogeneous maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$.

Licci ideals are ideals that can be linked by a finite number of steps to a complete intersection.

All licci ideals admit a rigid deformation, and two licci ideals are said to be in the same Herzog class if they have a common rigid deformation.

Guerrieri-Ni-Weyman gave a parametrization for the Herzog classes of codimension $3$ licci ideals in terms of pairs of partitions associated to Schur functors.

In this paper, we give an explicit formula that determines the Herzog class of a given $\mathfrak{m}$-primary licci monomial ideal.

items.title: Embedding into quotient
items.summary:
We study Bass's finiteness problem for embeddings into proper quotients. Given a commutative ring R, a reduced finitely generated R-algebra A, and an ideal $J\triangleleft A$, we ask whether an R-algebra monomorphism $A\hookrightarrow_R A/J$ forces J=0.

We give affirmative answers by presenting two arguments. Also, we discuss not only in the reduced case, but also in several non-reduced cases: when R is artinian and A is finite over R; when R is zero-dimensional and A is finite projective over R; and in a series of Cohen--Macaulay settings.

In the module-theoretic direction, for a noetherian reduced ring, and a finitely generated, and torsion-free A-module M, we show that $M\hookrightarrow_R M/JM$ implies that J is contained in a minimal prime of A; if M is faithful, then J=0. Also, dual versions investigated.

Examples illustrate the necessity of hypotheses.

items.title: Classification of all non-split central extensions of naturally graded 2-filiform non-Lie Leibniz algebras
items.summary:
This paper deals with the naturally graded 2-filiform non-Lie Leibniz algebras over the field of complex numbers. There are two finite series of such algebras, defined in every dimension starting from five, and two further algebras which occur only in dimension five.

For each of these algebras we classify, up to isomorphism, all of its non-split central extensions, of every possible dimension. The one-dimensional central extensions are already known from an earlier work, so the main part of the paper is devoted to the extensions of dimension two and higher.

As usual, the classification is reduced to the description of the orbits of the automorphism group of the algebra on the subspaces of its second cohomology space with trivial coefficients. For each algebra and each dimension we give the complete list of these orbits together with the multiplication tables of the corresponding algebras, and we point out the extensions whose annihilator coincides with the added central ideal.

Among the algebras obtained there are 2-filiform Leibniz algebras which are not naturally graded; this class of algebras has not been systematically studied so far.

items.title: Principal bundles in supersymmetry
items.summary:
We discuss rather basic problems on super principal bundles for $C^{\infty}$-supermanifolds (over $\mathbb{R}$) and analytic supermanifolds over a complete field of arbitrary characteristic.

Sharper answers are obtained for $C^{\infty}$-supermanifolds and for homogeneous supermanifolds.

Among others, it is proved for $C^{\infty}$-supermanifolds that given a $C^{\infty}$-supermanifold $B$ and a super Lie group $G$, there is a natural one-to-one correspondence (up to isomorphism) between the $G$-super principal bundles over $B$ and the $G_{\mathrm{rd}}$-principal bundles over $B_{\mathrm{rd}}$, where $G_{\mathrm{rd}}$ (resp., $B_{\mathrm{rd}}$) denotes the ordinary Lie group (resp., manifold) associated with $G$ (resp., $B$).

To prove this, we show a generalized, equivariant version of the renowned Batchelor Theorem.

items.title: 2-Local Derivations on Conformal Galilei Lie Algebras and Their Central Extensions
items.summary:
We classify 2-local derivations on the finite-dimensional conformal Galilei Lie algebras in three natural settings: the algebra without central extension, the mass central extension, and the exotic central extension. No additivity or linearity is assumed in the definition of a 2-local derivation.

We prove that in every case each 2-local derivation is an ordinary derivation. For the unextended algebra, the proof combines characteristic-quotient normalization with separating vectors, invariant bilinear forms, rank-two mixed zero anchors, and a semisimple-perturbation argument for the standard module.

For the mass central extension with $2\ell\ge3$, the residual map is first reduced to the center and then eliminated by a symplectic-anchor construction on the Heisenberg radical; a dimension argument in the centralizer of a regular semisimple element simultaneously handles singular reductive actions and the additional central shear that occurs in spatial dimension two. The endpoint $\ell=\tfrac12$ is the Schrödinger algebra; a self-contained symplectic-anchor proof includes all spatial dimensions, with explicit treatment of dimensions one and two.

For the exotic extension, after center normalization we use conjugate middle-weight positions and an affine middle anchor to eliminate every central translate, including the one-sided middle-weight configurations. Consequently the set of 2-local derivations coincides with the derivation algebra for all admissible parameters, and hence every 2-local derivation in these families is automatically linear.

items.title: On the arithmetic rank and cohomological dimension of some residual intersections
items.summary:
We determine the arithmetic rank and cohomological dimension of each generic residual intersection of the ideal of submaximal Pfaffians of an alternating matrix of variables. This ideal fails to be a set-theoretic complete intersection.

Our methods yield several structural results: in characteristic zero, we compute the $D$-module length of the top local cohomology module supported at this ideal and show that over the integers, it admits a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space structure. In particular, the top local cohomology module has no integer torsion.

We also establish the $F$-regularity of the generic residual intersection rings considered here. Further, for each admissible height $s$, we construct $s$-residual intersections of complete intersection ideals and height three Gorenstein ideals that are set-theoretic complete intersections in any characteristic.

Finally, we pose a general question of independent interest concerning the behaviour of arithmetic rank.

items.title: Non-existence of negative weight derivations on Jacobian algebras
items.summary:
Let $S=\mathbb K[x_1,\cdots,x_n]$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables with positive integer weights over a field $\mathbb K$ of characteristic zero.

Let $f\in S$ be a weighted homogeneous polynomial such that the Jacobian algebra $$A=\left.S \middle/ \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},\cdots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\right)\right.$$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb K$-vector space.

We prove that $A$ has no nonzero negative weight derivation, which confirms a conjecture of the third author.

An immediate consequence of this conjecture is the micro-local characterization of quasi-homogeneous singularities.

items.title: Achieving near-zero-downtime scaling in Elastic Expert Parallelism
items.summary:
How asynchronous preparation and NIXL EP enabled near-zero-downtime Elastic EP scaling in vLLM.

Traditionally, changing the number of GPUs in a vLLM service required adding or removing entire model replicas or restarting the engine with a different GPU count. As models grow larger, each replica needs more GPUs, so scaling by replica adds or removes GPUs in increasingly large increments. Restarting vLLM to scale DeepSeek V4 Pro from 16 to 20 GB200 GPUs stopped serving for 197 seconds (see the performance section for details), leaving those expensive GPUs allocated without generating tokens.

In our first Elastic EP post , we showed how vLLM could add or remove GPUs from a running DEP deployment (data-parallel attention with expert-parallel MoE) without restarting it. While we avoided a restart, serving still stopped throughout reconfiguration as we initialized new workers, prepared the expanded communication groups, loaded model weights, and repeated kernel warmup and CUDA graph capture. In our DeepSeek V4 Pro benchmark, this pause lasted 100 seconds when scaling from 16 to 20 GPUs and 56 seconds when scaling back to 16 GPUs (full details in the performance section ).

In this post, we describe how asynchronous preparation and NIXL EP enabled Elastic EP reconfiguration with near-zero downtime. In the same benchmark, we reduced downtime to 0.82 seconds when scaling from 16 to 20 GPUs and 1.96 seconds when scaling back to 16 GPUs , allowing us to scale up and down with almost no impact on serving performance.

We reorganized vLLM's reconfiguration flow into two phases: background preparation and a short commit. Existing workers use separate background threads to prepare and warm up target communication, transfer model weights, and synchronize execution-related information (such as autotuning results) with joining workers, while continuing to serve requests with their current communication groups and CUDA graphs. In parallel, joining workers initialize, receive model weights, and prepare their communication and GPU execution. During the commit phase, vLLM briefly pauses its schedulers, activates the prepared topology, and resumes serving. These changes were introduced in asynchronous preparation and prepare/commit optimizations .

items.title: Lefschetz Properties of complete intersesctions and maximal variation of hyperplane sections
items.summary:
For an artinian complete intersection of forms of degree $d$, we prove that the multiplication by a general linear form is injective up to degree $\frac{3d-1}2$, independently of the number of variables.

This is accomplished using algebraic and geometric properties of the union of two complete intersection curves and their general hyperplane sections.

As a consequence, we solve, for any $d\ge 4$, the problem about the maximal variation of the hyperplane sections of a smooth hypersurface of degree $d$ posed by A.

Beauville.

items.title: Polynomial bounds for the stability of associated primes of monomial ideals
items.summary:
Let $I$ be a nonzero proper monomial ideal in ${\rm k}[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$, and let $d$ be the maximal degree of a minimal monomial generator. We prove that the index of stability of the associated primes of its ordinary powers satisfies \[ {\rm astab}(I)\le\frac{(4e)^{r-1}}4\,d^{r-1}\qquad(r\ge3), \] while ${\rm astab}(I)=1$ for $r=2$.

If $I$ has $s\ge2$ minimal generators, we also obtain \[ {\rm astab}(I)\le\min\{r,s\}(s-1)d^{\min\{r-1,s-2\}}. \] The first estimate answers Hoa's question on polynomial bounds. The proofs reduce stabilization to integer optimization for a matrix whose last row records the power of the ideal.

We bound the degrees of its circuits and Graver basis elements and prove proximity estimates for optimal solutions in fixed fibers. A Steinitz rearrangement and a lattice-point count in the difference body of a simplex give the generator-independent bound.

The matrix estimates hold for arbitrary indexed integral configurations in a simplex and real linear objective functions. The stability bounds hold over an arbitrary field, without normality or equigeneration assumptions.

items.title: Will it be a golden age or a dark age for mathematics (and science)?
items.summary:
[This is a guest post by Francesco Maggi . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

Large language models (LLMs) and the research systems built around them (and commonly known as “artificial intelligence”) have demonstrated remarkable abilities in generating mathematical proofs. While the quality and limits of these tools remain incompletely understood, their potential for accelerating discovery and enabling extraordinary advances in mathematics and, more broadly, across science and technology seems clear.

Seizing on that potential will require the careful integration of LLMs into the various STEM ecosystems, with the priorities of empowering a new generation of scientists, developing new STEM expertise, and preserving an open, collaborative, and intellectually independent scientific enterprise: that is the “golden age” scenario in the title. In the “dark age” scenario, scientific and technological output would still increase spectacularly in the short term, but, at the same time, independent human scientific activity would progressively weaken, the production of new knowledge becoming increasingly concentrated in a small number of hands, who become increasingly incapable of understanding the knowledge produced. The real darkness here would be knowledge becoming alien to human understanding.

Reality will likely combine these scenarios. In eight points, I will examine the choices shaping that outcome, moving from mathematics to science more broadly, and closing with actionable proposals.

(1) The technological breakthrough is real! But…

To state the obvious, LLMs have become powerful research tools. Recent LLM-generated proofs, like the construction of a finite-time blow-up solution to the Navier–Stokes equations with a forcing term, or the proposed proof of the quasi-Riemann Hypothesis, deserve the utmost attention from mathematicians. Assessing their significance will require continuous independent scrutiny, interpretation, and assimilation by the mathematical community.

LLMs seem most at home when writing proofs in Lean. (Lean is a proof assistant that allows computers to check whether a formal argument establishes a stated claim under specified definitions and axioms.) For those hard theorems where we really want LLMs to help us, these Lean proofs are extremely long, like hundreds of thousands of lines of code long. A seemingly emergent trend is that the longer the Lean version of a proof, the messier and less faithful its machine-generated “natural language” translation seems to be. We don’t understand why LLMs seem so bad at doing this kind of translation, but, as of today, they seem to really struggle with that task. So, for the really important problems, LLMs can give us correct Lean proofs that we cannot directly read, and messy natural language translations that are so complex as to require intensive study by mathematicians before they can lead to human understanding. Although this specific problem translation problem may change in the future, it leads us directly to the fundamental question:

items.title: Rank and Border Rank Additivity of Complex Tensors with a Hankel Summand
items.summary:
We prove that the CP rank of a complex Hankel tensor of order $m\ge3$ is additive with that of every complex tensor of the same order.

Together with the known equality of CP and symmetric ranks for complex Hankel tensors, this yields symmetric rank additivity whenever the other summand has equal CP and symmetric ranks.

We also prove that ordinary and symmetric border ranks coincide and are additive on direct sums of complex Hankel tensors of any common order at least three.

Their common value is the sum of the middle binary catalecticant ranks.

For order three, we further prove border-rank additivity when the other summand has border rank at most three, or is symmetric with at most five essential variables.

items.title: Starting a new journal
items.summary:
[This is a guest post by Shaoming Guo – T.]

Several math colleagues and I are preparing to launch a new journal. As we considered which values we wanted the journal to uphold, we realized that there may be many other values worth exploring as a community, potentially through the creation of additional journals. We would like to use Terry’s blog to open a discussion of these possibilities. There are many dimensions to this discussion: what journals should aim to accomplish, what kinds of mathematical contributions they should recognize and reward, how papers should be evaluated, and how mathematical knowledge can best be communicated and made reliable. As new tools change the way mathematics is developed and shared, we have an opportunity to reconsider long standing conventions and imagine new possibilities for mathematical publishing.

For the journal we are currently planning, we envision two core values (in additional to traditional values like open access):

Prioritizing understanding over being first. We place far greater value on how much a paper deepens our understanding of its results and proofs than on whether it provides the first proof of those results.

Ensuring rigor through formal verification. As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to develop mathematical proofs, the potential for subtle, hard-to-detect errors is a growing concern. To be accepted, a paper will need to have its proofs formally verified in Lean.

Alongside feedback on this proposal, we welcome ideas for substantially different visions of future journals: the values they might uphold, the needs they might serve, and the practices they might adopt. A single journal is unlikely to accommodate every worthwhile idea, and combining too many requirements could place excessive constraints on authors. We hope this discussion will inspire a variety of new journals and other platforms, allowing the community to explore different approaches to the future of mathematical publishing.

items.title: Every commutative perfect ring is a quotient of an almost perfect domain
items.summary:
In this paper, we show that every nonzero commutative perfect ring is a quotient of a one-dimensional semilocal almost perfect domain of characteristic zero. The domain can be chosen to have as many maximal ideals as the given ring has local factors.

The construction uses coefficient discrete valuation rings, triangular presentations of purely inseparable residue extensions, and approximation for finitely many independent rank-one valuations. Independent error variables keep the construction inside a field.

A normal-form argument shows that the divided elements used to get perfect principal quotients do not kill any further good monomial. In positive residue characteristic, the choice $a=2c+1$ with $c\ge n$ protects the nonzero powers of $p$ in a target ring of characteristic $p^n$.

We also give local and mixed-characteristic consequences, and examples with non-nilpotent radicals.

items.title: On the classification of threefold flops
items.summary:
We show that possibly singular threefold flopping contractions are completely classified by their associated derived contraction algebras, considered up to derived Morita equivalence; in contrast to the smooth case the extra derived structure is necessary in general.

This extends previous work of the author on simple flops, and follows from a more general theorem about isolated hypersurface singularities.

The key new input is to show that derived localisation at a Hochschild class is Morita invariant; this result raises some interesting questions related to the classification of recollements.

We also show that derived contraction algebras admit a deformation-theoretic interpretation in families in a general setting that encompasses threefold flops, flips, and divisor-to-curve contractions.

items.title: Unique Factorization of Power Series Rings over Q-UFDs of Dimension at Most 3
items.summary:
Let $R$ be a Noetherian unique factorization domain containing $\mathbb Q$, with $\dim R\leq3$.

We prove that $R[[t]]$ is a unique factorization domain if and only if two conditions hold: every two-generated parameter ideal $q$ in every height-two localization satisfies $\overline{q^2}\subseteq q$, and every height-three localization has depth three.

No excellence or completion hypothesis is imposed.

The main local result is that $A[[t]]$ is not a UFD whenever $A$ is a local $\mathbb Q$-UFD of dimension at least three and depth two.

We also prove that the UFD property of $R[[t]]$ passes to every coefficient localization in dimension at most three, give an all-dimensional criterion when the completions of the maximal localizations satisfy Serre's condition $(S_2)$, and obtain an arbitrary-characteristic criterion for excellent UFDs of dimension at most three.

items.title: Bounded powers of edge ideals: Nearly Gorenstein polytopes
items.summary:
A lattice polytope $\mathcal{P} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ of dimension $n$ is called nearly Gorenstein if $\mathcal{P}$ is normal and if its Ehrhart ring is a nearly Gorenstein ring.

We study nearly Gorenstein polytopes arising from discrete polymatroids of bounded powers of edge ideals.

Especially, it is shown that every nearly Gorenstein polytope coming from either a complete graph or a complete bipartite graph is level.

items.title: Sumsets regularity versus Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity for monomial curves
items.summary:
Let $A=\{0=a_0<a_1<\dots<a_{k-1}=d\}$ be integers with greatest common divisor $1$, let $C_A$ be the projective monomial curve they define, and let $\mathrm{reg}(A)$ be the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of its coordinate ring. Gimenez and González-Sánchez proved $\mathrm{reg}(A)\leσ(A)+1$ for the sumsets regularity $σ(A)$; the reverse inequality $σ(A)\le\mathrm{reg}(A)$ was proposed as an open conjecture in a 2024 talk.

We show that it fails and measure by how much. Let $c_1,c_2$ be the conductors of the two numerical semigroups attached to $A$ and $N=\lceil(c_1+c_2)/d\rceil$.

For curves in $\mathbb{P}^3$ that are not arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay, $\mathrm{reg}(A)\ge(c_1+c_2)/d+2$, with equality exactly for the arithmetically Buchsbaum curves, and $σ(A)=\mathrm{reg}(A)$. For arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay curves in $\mathbb{P}^3$ we prove $9N\le10\,\mathrm{reg}(A)-2$, with $9/10$ best possible, and give an explicit family with $σ(A)-\mathrm{reg}(A)$ unbounded.

In $\mathbb{P}^4$ a family with a band-shaped Apéry set has $\mathrm{reg}(A)/σ(A)\to(2+\sqrt2)/4$ along the solutions of a Pell equation, and gluing carries this bound to every $\mathbb{P}^r$ with $r\ge5$.

items.title: SAIR Open Math OS released
items.summary:
As announced a few weeks ago , the SAIR Open Math OS is now soft launched . It offers services and web interfaces similar to frontier AI models, though currently we are hosting existing open math models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3, and GLM 5.3 Flash) which are roughly a year or so behind the current frontier models in capability; so not able to perform “one-shot problem solving” of the type we have heard frequently about in recent months, but capable enough for many other useful mathematical tasks, such as medium-sized Lean formalization, or summarizing or discussing a mathematical argument or topic. Here is a typical screenshot:

We are in the process of gathering partners to develop a more fine-tuned model for mathematics by post-training on an existing open model; see this link (and the associated Zulip channel ) for more details.

One feature of our model is the emphasis on team accounts rather than individual accounts, in which members of a team see each other’s prompts. We believe this could be a better format for using these tools for collaborative projects.

We are hosting these models using donated compute, and are in the process of granting free accounts to requesters from academic institutions. We may need to adjust the allocation of compute depending on demand and on future donations, but we will try to make the models available to as many users as possible.

This is still a very early version of the model; we accelerated our timeline for first release due to the increased demand for open models from the community. We will continue developing the model and accompanying features and welcome feedback, for instance at the Zulip channel .

items.title: LCM Splittings in GCD Domains
items.summary:
In a GCD ring $R$, every pair of elements $a,b\in R$ admits a greatest common divisor $\text{gcd}(a,b)$ and a least common multiple $\text{lcm}(a,b)$.

Motivated by a question on Mathematics Stack Exchange by Ash Seifert~\cite{Sei22}, I introduce the notion of an lcm splitting $c,d\in R$ for $a,b$ satisfying $cd\sim\text{lcm}(a,b), c\mid a, d\mid b, \text{gcd}(c,d)\sim1$.

I show that adequate Bézout domains always admit lcm splittings, give examples of Bézout domains in which some pair has no lcm splitting, and make further remarks on this seemingly new property.

items.title: Dg models for derived differential operators
items.summary:
We show that for any algebra $R$ that is essentially of finite type over a field $k$, the derived functors of Smith-Van den Bergh admit a dg enhancement.

In particular, for any $R$-module $M$ one can associate a dg algebra of differential operators $E_M$ whose cohomology is a nilpotent thickening of the (classical) ring of $k$-linear differential operators on $M$.

We show that these dg algebras fit into a framework of Koszul duality due to Dwyer-Greenlees and specializes to a derived ring of differential operators studied by Yang when $M=R$ and $k=\mathbb{C}$.

In particular, upon fixing a presentation $R=S/I$ with $S$ essentially smooth, we show a derived Kashiwara's equivalence, namely that whenever $\mathrm{supp}_S(M)=\mathrm{V}(I)$ then there is an equivalence of triangulated categories between the derived category of dg ${E}_M$-modules and the derived category of $D$-modules on $S$ that are set-theoretically supported on $I$.

Finally, in the case of positive characteristic, we show that the dg algebra ${E}_M$ admits a description in terms of the Frobenius endomorphism akin to the classical description of differential operators, and the proof employs simplicial techniques to obtain a result of independent interest in commutative algebra.

items.title: Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: Moving Fast and Responsibly
items.summary:
How agent-assisted CuTe DSL optimizations accelerate Kimi K3 decode on NVIDIA GB300, and how scoped changes, correctness tests, and reproducible benchmarks help ship them responsibly.

Coding agents can now help with some of the hardest parts of model optimization: writing complex GPU kernels, performing cross-operator fusions, overlapping computation with communication, and tuning execution across different batch sizes and GPU configurations. For Kimi K3, we used agent-assisted development to build a unified CuTe DSL decode path on the NVIDIA GB300, covering attention, MoE, and communication across 8 or 16 GPUs. The optimizations deliver over 840 tokens/s at batch 1 on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with DSpark (synthetic AL=6), 1.5–2× higher decode throughput in several tested configurations, and up to 1.8× higher P90 interactivity on the AgentX workload.

Agent-optimized inference code is outpacing our review and maintenance workflow. The manual review process of understanding every line of every kernel, mapping out potential issues, and testing every supported configuration, is very time-consuming work. On the other hand, if we omit this work then we risk shipping buggy software that could fail in production.

There is a clear line-of-sight on how to achieve both goals: we need to change how we organize performance work. Alongside agentic optimization, we need to design systems that allow automatic verification of reliability and performance, and we need to structure the software to enforce isolation and risk minimization by design.

The proposed fast-track model optimization RFC provides a foundation for this approach. Our guiding principle is to decrease review burden while managing risk . To accomplish this, we:

items.title: Scaling Kimi K3 on AMD Instinct MI355X: Matching NVIDIA HGX B300 Throughput per GPU on AgentX
items.summary:
Inside the Kimi K3 optimization effort: understanding the bottlenecks and the decisions that made inference faster

On AgentX, an eight-GPU AMD Instinct MI355X system serving Kimi K3 with vLLM delivers 24.4% more total tokens per second per GPU than NVIDIA HGX B300 at 50 tokens/s/user P90 interactivity. Under the benchmark’s ownership-cost model, it delivers 87.4% more tokens per dollar .

In this post, we’ll unpack the engineering behind Kimi K3 on AMD Instinct MI355X, connecting vLLM’s serving decisions to GPU kernels and the hardware underneath. We’ll explain why the optimizations worked and build the intuition to spot wasted work, identify bottlenecks and find the next optimization in your own inference stack.

Interactivity is reciprocal P90 response inter-token latency and excludes time to first token. Total tokens include reused input and generated output.

Source: SemiAnalysis InferenceX , October 9, 2026 snapshot. Comparison configurations .

items.title: Push-Based KV Transfer to Improve TTFT and TPOT for Disaggregated Inference in vLLM
items.summary:
A push-based NIXL connector for vLLM disaggregated serving: the prefill instance writes KV directly into decode memory over RDMA, taking the router relay, decode-side allocation, and transfer setup off the TTFT critical path.

vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT).

One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over RDMA-capable interconnects such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA, enabling NIXL to transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.

This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. For customers running disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, this can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.

In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30% better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for Qwen3-32B model; results depend on workload and configuration.

items.title: Finish RL Training Faster: Bitwise-Consistent, High-Performance, Agent-Driven
items.summary:
We make vLLM rollout and the training forward give bitwise identical logprobs on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (NVFP4), keep 91% of rollout throughput on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and open-source the agent skill.

DeepSeek-V4-Flash reached 0 diff first; the process became an agent skill, which was then applied to Nemotron-3.5 (a Mamba-2 hybrid). Left: DeepSeek-V4-Flash train-inference KL; the baseline climbs from 2e-3 to 29.9 and the consistent run is 0 at every step. Right: Nemotron-3.5 train score on SWE-bench Pro (5-step rolling mean); the consistent run stays around 0.6 while the baseline falls to 0.23.

Rollout dominates RL training time, so training systems adopt low-precision compute, low-precision KV cache, and communication and kernel optimizations. These change the inference-side numerics. The inference engine generates a response; the training engine recomputes its probabilities and updates the model. With identical weights, the two sides now assign different probabilities to the same token, so training optimizes a policy other than the one that sampled. The gap can grow with updates and destabilize training. In our DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base experiment (no algorithmic correction such as TIS), the high-performance baseline's train-inference KL rose from 2e-3 to 29.9 while reward fell back.

Unstable training means more crashes, rollbacks and reruns, a smaller share of effective training, and more total time to reach the same result. Our goal is to finish effective RL training faster : by cutting crashes and reruns, reach a result in less end-to-end time.

Our approach: on the high-performance numerical path, training and inference produce a bitwise identical logprob for every sampled token (diff = 0; Section 2 defines it exactly), which is true on-policy RL. We get there by having the training forward call vLLM's inference kernels directly and modifying those high-performance kernels so results do not change with batch composition, prefill or decode phase, or parallel layout (Sections 3 and 4). An agent skill then lowers the cost of doing this on a new model and makes the process transferable: it tells an agent how to find the first operator where the two sides diverge, reduce it to a minimal repro, fix it and rerun the regressions. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash we reach 0 diff at 91.3% of the high-performance baseline's rollout throughput, and we carried the method over to Nemotron, a Mamba hybrid with NVFP4.

items.title: Adaptive Verification Without a Confidence Head
items.summary:
An online-fitted acceptance estimator that lets every draft-model speculator use Adaptive Verification, by predicting the target's acceptance probability from the drafter's own logits and refitting continuously during serving.

Confidence scoring is now supported for all draft-model-based speculator types. In the absence of a confidence head, an online-fitted estimator derives a feature from the drafter's logits to predict the target model's probability of accepting it, which is used directly as a confidence score for Adaptive Verification. The estimator's coefficients are continuously fitted, adapting to the incoming data traffic. This feature landed in PR #52228 , and is enabled with enable_adaptive_verification for draft models without a confidence head.

vLLM's Adaptive Verification (AV) enables verification of a subset of the drafted tokens during speculative decoding. Draft tokens with low probability of acceptance are trimmed from the batch before running the target model's forward pass, saving on compute. This optimization is particularly beneficial while serving large batch sizes, because in that regime the GPU becomes compute-bound. See this vLLM blog post for more details.

AV needs a per-token estimate of acceptance probability, which is why, until now, it only supported DSpark drafters. DSpark models often ship with a confidence head: a small linear layer over the drafter's hidden state for each position, trained as a binary classifier for "will the target accept this token?"

Draft models that lack a confidence head, such as EAGLE, MTP, DFlash, and some DSpark checkpoints, miss out on AV entirely. To use it, these drafters need a per-token acceptance estimate, and adding a confidence head means retraining the drafter, which isn't an option for the many existing checkpoints that people already serve.

items.title: Improve TTFT for Multi-Turn Agentic Workloads with Bi-Directional KV Transfer in vLLM
items.summary:
Bi-directional KV transfer lets vLLM prefill nodes reuse previously computed KV from decode nodes on later conversation turns, cutting redundant prefill recompute and reducing TTFT by up to 3.3x on long multi-turn prompts.

Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its KV cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response.

Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes do not, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT).

For customers building conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer enables prefill and decode nodes to reuse previously computed context across turns, improving accelerator utilization and helping applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow.

In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS), bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section); results depend on workload and configuration.

New Model additions

Nemotron 3 Diarization

Nemotron 3 Diarization is an open-weight streaming speaker diarization model designed to determine "who spoke when" in real-world audio. It supports both streaming and offline inference, handles up to eight speakers, and orders speaker outputs by each speaker's first arrival in the input audio.

The model uses the Arrival-Order Speaker Cache (AOSC) 1 and FIFO queue introduced for Streaming Sortformer 1 , 2 . A single checkpoint supports configurable latency profiles, from an 80 ms input buffer to a 30.4 s offline-style buffer, and configurable output frame resolution in multiples of 10 ms. With chunked inference, the maximum audio duration is not limited.

items.title: Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words to Jev
items.summary:
The recently released Jev AI model has been quite a cultural phenomenon in technical communities in the past 2 weeks.

While Jev aims to classify things, it’s easy to dismiss Jev as “just a classifier,” and my own view of Jev has evolved quite a bit over the past few days. In particular, my thoughts went from “classifiers used to be my bread & butter; I can easily build this myself” (more on this later) to “wow, this actually works better than I thought.”

Figure 1: Quick overview of the Jev API; more details on that later.

Sure, the latest state-of-the-art GPT and open-weight LLMs can do the same kinds of classification tasks as Jev, while also being capable of much more general decision-making. But Jev’s advantage is that it can handle those classification tasks much faster and more cheaply.

At the other end of the spectrum, for a narrow, well-defined problem, Jev probably won’t classify anything better, faster, or cheaper than a special-purpose classifier. But its selling point is that it is far more general than those task-specific models.

So, what is the methodology behind Jev (based on an educated guess), what can it do, and why is it so popular? I aim to answer all of these later in this article. However, I thought starting with a brief history of language models for decision-making would be a great way to begin. And it hopefully helps demystify some of the hype and show what Jev does very well (”Jev is essentially a text classifier,” but “Jev is also not ‘just’ a text classifier.”)

PS: I am not affiliated with Jev in any way. Also, I am not offered free access to Jev, and this is also not a product endorsement, just a technical article to offer some insights into the history of text classification to help you make sense of the recent hype.

items.title: Taking vLLM Apart: A Practical Guide to Disaggregated Serving
items.summary:
What disaggregated serving actually buys you, how to run it end to end in vLLM today with prefill/decode plus the new GPU-less frontend and the things we're still working on.

A single vllm serve process does three jobs that get in each other's way: processing prompts (prefill), generating tokens (decode) and a pile of CPU work around them. Disaggregated serving in vLLM separates the different stages of LLM inference. Splitting prefill from decode stops long prompts stalling everyone else's output, as long as the KV cache moves between them fast. Moving tokenization and parsing to a CPU-only frontend ( /render , /derender ) takes that work off your GPU nodes and leaves the engine working purely in token IDs. This post covers when each split or separation is worth using, how to run it with vLLM v0.31.0 or later, and the key gaps and improvements still ahead.

Start a plain vllm serve and you get one process handling three workloads that have nothing in common.

One long prompt arrives while dozens of requests are mid-response and every one of those streams stutters until it's processed. It's the spike you see the moment concurrency goes up. The cause is two phases with little in common sharing one GPU. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass, is limited by compute and sets your time to first token (TTFT). Decode is the opposite. It produces one token at a time and what holds it back is how fast the GPU can read the model weights from memory which sets your inter-token latency (ITL). Put them on the same GPU and every decode stream waits while a long prefill runs.

The third job however is quieter and easier to miss. Chat templating, tokenization, detokenization, reasoning parsing, tool call parsing. All pure CPU work running on a box you're renting for its accelerators.

items.title: Watermarking in vLLM
items.summary:
How vLLM implements distribution-preserving Gumbel-max text watermarking with efficient GPU kernels, statistical detection, speculative decoding, and repeated-context safeguards.

Establishing the provenance of digital content is essential to build trust and accountability in the information we share. Watermarking offers a solution: it alters a work to embed a message about it [1] , for instance its provenance. Images and audio can embed watermarks as a subtle perturbation, but these techniques are not applicable to text due to its discrete nature. Instead of trying to perturb the text itself, we influence the generation process in a way that is detectable but does not modify the expected output distribution.

Watermarking text is both a scientific and engineering challenge, and there are several requirements that we must aim to balance to have a practical solution:

Adding a watermark should not modify the expected output distribution of a model [2] : it should not systematically favour certain words, writing styles, or solutions to problems.

Generated text can be altered in many ways: shortened, edited, mixed with other corpora, or even rephrased by another LLM. A good watermarking system aims to preserve its provenance signal even under such modification.

items.title: Announcing vllm-metal: Concurrent Serving on Apple Silicon
items.summary:
vllm-metal brings vLLM's paged, continuously batched serving stack to Apple Silicon, with flatter TTFT under concurrent agent load, batched MTP, and automatic M5 prefill acceleration.

Local inference on a Mac is straightforward until several requests overlap. Then time to first token (TTFT), memory growth, and admission control become serving problems rather than model-execution problems. vllm-metal brings vLLM's scheduler, paged KV cache, and OpenAI-compatible server to Apple Silicon, with MLX and Metal handling execution.

Our first official release, v0.28.0 , aligned vllm-metal's version numbering with upstream vLLM. It introduced batched multi-token prediction (MTP), GGUF and hybrid-model support, and faster prefill on M5. You can install v0.29.0 with Homebrew .

vllm-metal plugs into upstream vLLM. vLLM provides the V1 scheduler, paged KV block management, chunked prefill, sampling, and the OpenAI-compatible frontend with streaming and tool-call parsing. mlx_lm provides the model implementations; MLX executes them.

At the model level, vllm-metal reuses mlx_lm's weight loading, RMSNorm, linear, MoE, and MLP layers unchanged. Those layers process each token independently, so they run on a packed token axis without knowing request boundaries. Attention does need those boundaries, so vllm-metal replaces stock attention with a paged varlen Metal kernel. Most of the plugin's model-specific code therefore sits in one layer.

items.title: Reducing vLLM startup time with one uv flag
items.summary:
Shipping Python bytecode saved about 18 seconds per startup in H100 server benchmarks, with images and models already local.

Fresh vLLM containers can spend seconds compiling Python source before serving any requests. Shipping that bytecode in the image saved about 18 seconds per startup in my H100 server benchmarks , with one uv build setting:

Set the flag before installing runtime packages so uv compiles their Python source during the build. This avoids repeated compilation during imports shared across models. Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B are two examples: median paired startup savings were 17.6 and 17.8 seconds, respectively.

For official-image users, PR #55422 is already included in this CUDA nightly :

The change will be supported in official release images starting with v0.32.0 . Users of those images do not need to set the build flag themselves.

items.title: Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants
items.summary:
We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers , so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained , and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX , it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️ Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook Pro For non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF , developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub . Publishers such as Unsloth , LM Studio Community , and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate . Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

items.title: Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community
items.summary:
We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm . We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng , Prince , Yagil , and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

items.title: PD Serving of Qwen3.8-2.4T
items.summary:
How vLLM reaches 5K throughput and 180 interactivity on Qwen3.8-2.4T with GB300 NVL72 PD serving and how to reproduce results yourself.

In this blog post we present our latest performance results on PD serving of the Qwen3.8-2.4T model using vLLM on a GB300 NVL72 cluster on 8K/1K workload. In high throughput scenario vLLM achieved 5000 total token throughput per GPU, and 180 generated tokens per user in the low latency scenario — both presented on pareto frontier below. In this blog post we explain in detail how we achieved these results, and give precise srt-slurm recipes to allow anyone to verify and reproduce them using local serving. But what is more important — we describe our decision making process we used to create these recipes. This is even more important than the actual performance results, since it allows you to squeeze performance out of PD serving on vLLM for any model you desire.

Recently, we presented our Qwen3.5 PD serving results and showed that vLLM could reach 25K Total TPS/GPU. Straight after that, a new frontier Qwen-family model was released: Qwen3.8-2.4T. In this post, we turn to PD serving for Qwen3.8-2.4T and present the full pareto frontier.

In our previous Qwen3.5 study, we focused primarily on left part of pareto curve, where the goal was to maximize Total TPS/GPU. This time, we go further and build the complete pareto frontier, covering both its left (high throughput) and right (low latency) parts. In other words, besides throughput-oriented configurations, we also identify optimal PD recipes for maximizing interactivity, i.e. Gen TPS per user.

Just as importantly, this blog post is not only about the final numbers. We also break down the tuning process step by step: how we chose what to measure, how we identified bottlenecks, and how we iterated toward better PD configurations. Our aim is to make this workflow understandable and reusable for anyone trying to tune serving performance for any another model.

items.title: Scaling Multi-GPU Video Captioning with PyNvVideoCodec and vLLM
items.summary:
How to leverage NVIDIA Hardware Video Decoders to Achieve Multi-GPU Scaling in Video Captioning and Description tasks.

We are excited to announce support for hardware video decoding built into NVIDIA GPUs, allowing video captioning and labeling tasks previously bottlenecked by CPU to scale their throughput on datacenter-grade multi-GPU nodes.

Video captioning is a common task in many industries for describing what is taking place in a video. This enables autonomous vehicle (AV) training systems to describe and classify dangerous scenarios, to produce human-readable and searchable metadata, among other use cases.

Previously, vLLM processing of these datasets required sending videos which could only be decoded via the CPU-based OpenCV+FFMPEG backend. Running such Vision Language Models (VLMs) on multi-GPU nodes (one vLLM server per GPU) places stronger demand on the CPU to decode video frames before any VLM inference work can begin. Especially in the case of video captioning, where outputs are relatively short (100-200 tokens), the relative portion of time spent decoding videos is much larger, and CPU-based video decoding can quickly become a bottleneck, maxing out CPU cores even with just 2 or 4 GPUs.

By integrating PyNvVideoCodec , a python-based interface to NVIDIA hardware video decoders (also known as “NVDEC”), vLLM is able to shift this video decoding workload off of the CPU and remove the aforementioned bottleneck, enabling excellent scaling even up to 8 GPUs.

items.title: vLLM x Novita AI: Chord, Faster INT4 MoE for Kimi K2.x. Up to 1.3x on H200, 2.15x on Untuned B300
items.summary:
Novita AI has open-sourced Chord, a high-performance W4A16 MoE CUDA kernel for Kimi K2.x serving shapes, with a Humming-compatible indexed path and grouped SM90 operators.

Novita AI has open-sourced Chord , a high-performance W4A16 MoE CUDA operator for BF16 activations, INT4 weights and group-32 scales. Built for Kimi K2.x serving shapes, its indexed path exposes the Humming-compatible humming import root, selected with --quantization humming on compatible vLLM revisions. Integration of the grouped operators with vLLM's Humming backend is still a work in progress.

Measured per layer against public Humming's matching path:

Figure 1. Per-call latency against public Humming across the six measured scenarios, lower is better. Read each panel on its own: the B300 decode panel compares against an untuned Humming default because public Humming ships no SM100/SM103 tuning table, while every H200 panel is tuned-to-tuned. Chart from the Chord repository ; full tables in docs/performance.md .

The idea behind these numbers is that one W4A16 MoE kernel cannot be right for every request. Routed tokens per expert varies by orders of magnitude between prefill and decode, and it is that quantity, not total token count, that decides which schedule wins. Chord picks the schedule from the shape it is actually given.

items.title: vime × RL-Kernel × AMD: Bitwise Train–Rollout Consistency on ROCm
items.summary:
vime and RL-Kernel align selected-token logprobs bit for bit across Megatron training and vLLM rollout on AMD Instinct MI300X, with zero mismatches across 200 GRPO steps.

Training and rollout usually use different execution engines and operators. Even with the same model, weights, and inputs, differences in kernels, parallelism, and reduction order can produce different logprobs.

This is a long-standing issue in RL systems because it affects the importance ratio, rollout–training KL diagnostics, and clipping. Existing work has focused mainly on NVIDIA platforms, while systematic exploration on ROCm has been more limited.

Building on vime × RL-Kernel, this work aligns the Attention, FFN, logprob, and communication paths on AMD Instinct MI300X to achieve bitwise train–rollout consistency.

Concretely, the rollout engine generates token from prefix and records the rollout-side logprob . The training engine then recomputes the same token under the same weight version to obtain . We track the difference and the corresponding importance ratio .

items.title: Kimi K3 Performance Optimizations in vLLM: The Road to 2.8× Throughput
items.summary:
Kimi K3 serving optimizations across scheduling, KDA prefix caching, ReplaySSM state recovery, PD disaggregation and state offload, parallelism, MoE, and GPU kernels.

Day-0 support got Kimi K3 running in vLLM. Efficient serving required another pass across the stack. KDA recurrent state, LatentMoE, MXFP4 expert kernels, speculative decoding, and TP/PP each exposed different bottlenecks; scheduler limits and small tensor copies could matter as much as a large GEMM.

This post starts with the end-to-end result, then looks at four representative changes: adaptive speculative-token budgets, internal KDA prefix checkpoints, zero-copy mixed KDA batches, and deferred MXFP4 finalization. Also covered: ReplaySSM, prefill/decode disaggregation and cache offload, and decode context parallelism. The wider effort is tracked in Kimi K3 Performance Optimization #50587 .

Measured with an 8K/1K workload with TP8, eight tokens DSpark speculation. Concurrency 1, 4, and 16. Comparison from v0.27.1 to commit 82a85dc1 (0913), tested on B300 node (CUDA 13.3).

Note: Prefix caching was disabled in both runs because v0.27.1 had a known Kimi K3 prefix-caching issue fixed later.
